title: Jallianwala Bagh, Vaisakhi 1919
hook: British troops fire on an unarmed crowd in a walled garden in Amritsar, killing hundreds

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saragarhi, and your line, twenty-one held. Did you hold one small post today? Today we go to Amritsar, on its happiest day of the year, and something that happened there. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival, and for Sikhs it's the birthday of the Khalsa. In Amritsar it means crowds: families in from the villages, bright turbans and scarves, a visit to the Harmandir, food, music, fairs. On Vaisakhi afternoon in 1919, thousands of people gathered in a public garden a few minutes' walk from the Golden Temple. Some had come to hear speeches. Many had just come in from the festival to sit on the grass. Today: Jallianwala Bagh.
screen: `VAISAKHI IN AMRITSAR.` → `A GARDEN NEAR THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.` → `THOUSANDS ON THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: Bagh means garden. Jallianwala Bagh was an open ground in the middle of the city, closed in on all sides by the walls of houses, with only a few narrow ways in and out. That spring, Punjab was tense. There had been protests against new British laws allowing arrest without trial, two popular local leaders, one Hindu and one Muslim, had been arrested, and public meetings had been banned. Many in the garden that day, especially the visitors from villages, likely didn't know about the ban. The crowd was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, and it was unarmed. A British officer, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, arrived with troops, stationed them at the main entrance, and without giving any warning ordered them to fire into the crowd. The firing went on for about ten minutes, until the ammunition was nearly spent. People tried to climb the walls. Some jumped into a well to escape. The official British count was 379 killed; Indian estimates were far higher, around a thousand. Many more were wounded. Nobody knows the true number. The massacre shocked India and many in Britain. The poet Rabindranath Tagore gave back his knighthood in protest. Many historians see that afternoon as a turning point toward Indian independence. The garden is a memorial now. You can still see the bullet marks in the walls and the well. And for Sikhs, it gave their spring festival a second meaning. Every Vaisakhi, amid the celebration, the people of that afternoon are remembered.
screen: `BAGH — A GARDEN.` · `WALLED IN, WITH NARROW EXITS.` · `AN UNARMED CROWD, FIRED ON WITHOUT WARNING.` · `A TURNING POINT TOWARD INDEPENDENCE.` · then, large: `VAISAKHI, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one: a small steady flame. Let it stand for the people in the garden that afternoon, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, who came for a festival and didn't go home. You don't need to picture what happened. Just watch the flame, and let it be their light. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Jallianwala Bagh. The walled garden in Amritsar where, on Vaisakhi in 1919, British troops fired on an unarmed crowd, killing hundreds.
Your line: vaisakhi, remembered. Today, in the middle of something good, pause once to remember someone who isn't there to share it. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: The Jallianwala Bagh is a national memorial in Amritsar, near Harmandir Sahib; each year on 13 April, Vaisakhi, people gather there to remember those killed, and many Sikhs include them in their Vaisakhi remembrance.

what a scholar hears: 13 April 1919; about 1,650 rounds fired; official toll 379 (Hunter Committee), Indian National Congress inquiry estimated around 1,000; followed the Rowlatt Act protests and the arrests of Dr Satyapal and Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew.

sources.ref: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919, as recorded in history (Hunter Committee report, 1920)

notes: Figures: 379 official dead; Indian estimates about 1,000; about 1,650 rounds and about ten minutes of firing. Confirm.
The two arrested leaders were Dr Satyapal (Hindu) and Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew (Muslim); confirm.
Tagore renounced his knighthood in May 1919; confirm.
Tone deliberately non-graphic; the script names Dyer as the officer responsible but does not blame any people as a whole.
